sun.name: Sun
sun.description: The Sun is the star at the center of our Solar System. It is a nearly perfect sphere of hot plasma, with internal convective motion that generates a magnetic field. It accounts for about 99.86% of the total mass of the Solar System.

educational_content.how_it_works: Nuclear fusion in the core converts hydrogen to helium, releasing tremendous energy as light and heat.

mercury.name: Mercury
mercury.description: Mercury is the smallest planet in our Solar System and the closest to the Sun. It has no atmosphere and experiences extreme temperature variations between day and night.

educational_content.how_it_works: Mercury has a large iron core that generates a weak magnetic field. Its lack of atmosphere causes extreme temperature swings.

venus.name: Venus
venus.description: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and Earth's closest planetary neighbor. It has a thick, toxic atmosphere that traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, making it the hottest planet in our solar system.

educational_content.how_it_works: Dense carbon dioxide atmosphere creates extreme greenhouse effect, trapping solar heat and creating surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead.

earth.name: Earth
earth.description: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only astronomical object known to harbor life. It has one natural satellite, the Moon, and orbits the Sun at a distance of about 150 million kilometers.

educational_content.how_it_works: Earth's magnetic field protects it from solar wind. Its atmosphere provides oxygen and regulates temperature through the greenhouse effect.

moon.name: Moon
moon.description: Earth's only natural satellite and the fifth largest moon in the Solar System. The Moon stabilizes Earth's axial tilt and creates ocean tides through gravitational interaction.

educational_content.how_it_works: The Moon's gravitational pull creates tidal forces on Earth. It is tidally locked, always showing the same face to Earth.

mars.name: Mars
mars.description: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, known as the Red Planet due to iron oxide on its surface. It has been a primary target for exploration due to evidence of past water and potential for past or present life.

educational_content.how_it_works: Mars has polar ice caps, extinct volcanoes (including Olympus Mons, the largest in the solar system), and evidence of ancient river valleys suggesting past liquid water.

jupiter.name: Jupiter
jupiter.description: Jupiter is the largest planet in our Solar System, with a mass more than twice that of all other planets combined. It has a Great Red Spot, a massive storm larger than Earth.

educational_content.how_it_works: Jupiter's massive gravity protects inner planets from asteroid impacts. Its rapid rotation creates powerful atmospheric bands and storms.

saturn.name: Saturn
saturn.description: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second-largest in the Solar System. It is famous for its extensive ring system made of ice particles, rocky debris, and dust.

educational_content.how_it_works: Saturn's rings are made of countless particles ranging from tiny grains to house-sized chunks, held in place by gravitational interactions.

uranus.name: Uranus
uranus.description: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and has a unique sideways rotation. It appears blue-green due to methane in its atmosphere and has a system of faint rings.

educational_content.how_it_works: Uranus rotates on its side, likely due to a massive collision early in its history. Its extreme tilt causes unusual seasonal variations.

neptune.name: Neptune
neptune.description: Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet from the Sun. It has the strongest winds in the solar system, reaching speeds of 2,100 km/h, and appears deep blue due to methane.

educational_content.how_it_works: Neptune's internal heat drives the strongest winds in the solar system. Its Great Dark Spot is a storm system similar to Jupiter's Great Red Spot.

black_hole.name: Black Hole
black_hole.description: A region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Formed from the collapse of massive stars or found at galactic centers as supermassive black holes.
technical_specs: Supermassive: Millions to billions of solar masses

educational_content.how_it_works: Extreme gravity warps spacetime, creating an event horizon beyond which nothing can escape. Matter falling in releases tremendous energy.

orion_nebula.name: Orion Nebula
orion_nebula.description: A diffuse nebula in the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye in the constellation Orion. It is one of the brightest nebulae and a stellar nursery where new stars are being formed.

educational_content.how_it_works: Dense clouds of gas and dust collapse under gravity, forming protostars that eventually ignite nuclear fusion, creating new stars.

pulsar.name: Pulsar
pulsar.description: A highly magnetized rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation. Observable as pulses of radiation as the star rotates, acting as a cosmic lighthouse.

educational_content.how_it_works: Rapidly rotating neutron star emits radiation beams from its magnetic poles. As it rotates, these beams sweep across Earth like a lighthouse.

ceres.name: Ceres (Dwarf Planet)
ceres.description: The largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Classified as a dwarf planet and contains about one-third of the belt's total mass. Visited by NASA's Dawn spacecraft.

educational_content.how_it_works: Ceres likely has a rocky core and icy mantle, with possible subsurface water ocean. Bright spots on surface are salt deposits.

asteroid.name: Asteroid
asteroid.description: Rocky, airless remnants left over from the early formation of our solar system about 4.6 billion years ago. Most orbit between Mars and Jupiter in the main asteroid belt.
technical_specs: Size range: Meters to hundreds of km

educational_content.how_it_works: Asteroids are remnants from planetary formation that never coalesced into a planet, held in orbit by the Sun's gravity.

meteoroid.name: Meteoroid
meteoroid.description: Small rocky or metallic bodies in space, smaller than asteroids. When they enter Earth's atmosphere, they become meteors (shooting stars). If they reach the ground, they're called meteorites.
technical_specs: Size: Grain of sand to 1 meter

educational_content.how_it_works: Meteoroids travel through space until entering a planet's atmosphere, where friction causes them to heat up, glow, and often vaporize.

lunar_gateway.name: Lunar Gateway
lunar_gateway.description: A planned space station in lunar orbit intended to serve as a communication hub, science laboratory, short-term habitation module, and staging point for missions to the Moon and Mars. Part of NASA's Artemis program.

educational_content.how_it_works: Gateway will orbit the Moon in a unique trajectory that allows access to the entire lunar surface with minimal fuel, serving as a staging point for surface missions.

iss.name: International Space Station
iss.description: The ISS is a modular space station in low Earth orbit. It is a multinational collaborative project involving NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, and CSA. The station serves as a microgravity and space environment research laboratory.

educational_content.how_it_works: The ISS orbits Earth every 90 minutes at 28,000 km/h, providing a platform for scientific research in microgravity and testing technologies for deep space exploration.

dsn_antenna.name: Deep Space Network Antenna
dsn_antenna.description: The DSN consists of three facilities worldwide (California, Spain, Australia) equipped with large radio antennas used to communicate with spacecraft across the solar system. The 70-meter antennas are among the largest and most sensitive.

educational_content.how_it_works: Large parabolic dish antennas transmit commands and receive data from deep space missions using radio frequencies. Three global stations provide 24/7 coverage.

agena_target_vehicle.name: Agena Target Vehicle
agena_target_vehicle.description: The Agena was an uncrewed spacecraft used by NASA in the 1960s as a docking target for Gemini missions. It demonstrated orbital rendezvous and docking techniques critical for the Apollo moon program.

educational_content.how_it_works: Agena served as an orbital target for Gemini spacecraft to practice docking maneuvers necessary for lunar missions. Its engine could also boost the combined stack to higher orbits.

progress_ms.name: Progress Cargo Spacecraft
progress_ms.description: Progress is an automated, uncrewed cargo spacecraft developed by Russia to resupply the International Space Station with food, water, propellant, oxygen, and equipment. It can also boost the ISS orbit and dispose of waste.

educational_content.how_it_works: Progress uses the automated Kurs rendezvous system to dock with ISS. After unloading, it's filled with waste and burns up in Earth's atmosphere during reentry.

acrimsat.name: ACRIMSAT
acrimsat.description: The Active Cavity Radiometer Irradiance Monitor Satellite measures total solar irradiance to study the Sun's effect on Earth's climate. It provided critical data on solar variability and climate forcing.

educational_content.how_it_works: ACRIM III measures the total amount of solar radiation reaching Earth to track solar variability and its influence on climate change.

landsat.name: Landsat
landsat.description: Landsat satellites provide continuous Earth observation data since 1972, making it the longest-running enterprise for acquisition of satellite imagery of Earth. Critical for monitoring land use, resources, and environmental change.
technical_specs: Instruments: OLI (Operational Land Imager), TIRS (Thermal Infrared Sensor)

educational_content.how_it_works: Multi-spectral imaging captures Earth's surface in visible and infrared wavelengths, revealing information invisible to human eyes for environmental monitoring.
applications: Land use and land cover mapping

satellite_generic.name: Satellite
satellite_generic.description: An artificial object placed in orbit around Earth or another celestial body. Satellites serve various purposes including communications, navigation, Earth observation, weather monitoring, and scientific research.
technical_specs: Attitude control: Reaction wheels, magnetorquers, thrusters

educational_content.how_it_works: Satellites maintain orbit through balance of gravitational pull and orbital velocity. Onboard systems provide power, communication, orientation control, and mission-specific operations.

astronaut.name: Astronaut
astronaut.description: A person trained, equipped, and deployed by a space program to serve as a commander or crew member aboard a spacecraft. Astronauts conduct scientific research, maintain spacecraft systems, and perform spacewalks (EVAs).
technical_specs: Temperature control: Active liquid cooling garment

educational_content.how_it_works: Astronauts undergo extensive training in spacecraft systems, survival skills, spacewalk procedures, robotics, scientific research, and physical conditioning to adapt to microgravity.

turbofan_engine.name: Turbofan Engine
turbofan_engine.description: A turbofan engine is a type of jet engine that uses a ducted fan to accelerate air around the engine core. It provides high thrust efficiency and is commonly used in commercial aviation. The bypass air provides additional thrust while reducing noise and improving fuel efficiency.

educational_content.how_it_works: The fan draws in air, part goes through the core (combustion) and part bypasses it, creating efficient thrust.

rocket_engine.name: Rocket Engine
rocket_engine.description: A rocket engine generates thrust through the expulsion of high-velocity exhaust gases. It operates on Newton's third law, producing thrust in the opposite direction of exhaust flow. Commonly uses liquid or solid propellants and is essential for space launch vehicles.

educational_content.how_it_works: Combustion of propellants creates high-pressure gas that is expelled through a nozzle at supersonic speeds.

wing.name: Aircraft Wing
wing.description: An aircraft wing generates lift through its airfoil shape and pressure differential. Its curved upper surface creates lower pressure above and higher pressure below, producing upward force. Wings also house fuel tanks and control surfaces for flight stability.

educational_content.how_it_works: Airfoil shape creates pressure difference - lower pressure above, higher below, resulting in net upward lift force.

turbine_blade.name: Turbine Blade
turbine_blade.description: A turbine blade extracts energy from high-temperature gas flow in jet engines. These precision-engineered components must withstand extreme temperatures and rotational forces while efficiently converting thermal energy to mechanical rotation.

educational_content.how_it_works: Hot exhaust gases from combustion spin the turbine blades, which drive the compressor and fan via a shaft.

fuel_tank.name: Aerospace Fuel Tank
fuel_tank.description: Storage container for rocket propellant or aircraft fuel. Must maintain structural integrity under pressure while minimizing weight. Often insulated for cryogenic fuels and designed to prevent fuel sloshing during flight.

educational_content.how_it_works: Stores fuel under controlled pressure, with insulation for cryogenic liquids like liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen.

landing_gear.name: Landing Gear
landing_gear.description: Retractable wheels and shock absorbers for aircraft landing and takeoff. Consists of hydraulic struts, wheels, brakes, and retraction mechanisms. Designed to absorb landing impact and support aircraft weight on the ground.

educational_content.how_it_works: Hydraulic shock struts absorb landing impact energy. Wheels support weight, and hydraulic systems retract gear to reduce drag in flight.

cockpit.name: Aircraft Cockpit
cockpit.description: The pilot's control area containing instruments, displays, and flight controls. Modern cockpits feature glass displays, fly-by-wire systems, and integrated avionics for navigation, communication, and aircraft monitoring.

educational_content.how_it_works: Pilots use integrated displays and controls to monitor aircraft systems and manage flight. Fly-by-wire converts control inputs to electronic signals.

propeller.name: Aircraft Propeller
propeller.description: A rotating blade assembly that converts engine power into thrust by accelerating air backward. Propellers are highly efficient at lower speeds and are used in general aviation and turboprop aircraft.

educational_content.how_it_works: Propeller blades act as rotating wings, creating thrust by pushing air backward using their airfoil shape.

tail_section.name: Aircraft Tail Section
tail_section.description: The rear portion of an aircraft containing vertical and horizontal stabilizers for flight stability and control. Includes rudder and elevator control surfaces.

educational_content.how_it_works: Stabilizers provide aerodynamic stability. Rudder controls yaw (left-right), elevator controls pitch (up-down).
